course.title: Chess Mastery: From Beginner to Intermediate
course.description: A conversational 25-part course where you learn chess alongside GM Viktor Solovyov — a sharp-tongued, brilliant chess legend who teaches you everything from moving your first pawn to calculating complex combinations. Every lesson features dialogue, stories, and interactive text-based boards.

parts.partTitle: Part 1: The Board, the Pieces & Your First Move

blocks.value: Chapter 1: Meeting the Master

*You walk into a dimly lit chess club. The smell of old wood and coffee hangs in the air. At the far table sits an elderly man hunched over a board, moving pieces with the precision of a surgeon. He doesn't look up.*

**You:** "Excuse me, are you Grandmaster Solovyov? I was told you teach beginners."

**Viktor:** *looks up slowly, eyes sharp as a hawk's* "Teach? No. I correct mistakes. You will make thousands. Sit."

*You sit. He pushes a board toward you.*
**Viktor:** "Before you touch a piece, you must understand the battlefield. Chess is not a game. It is a **war on 64 squares**. The board is your world. Learn it."
The 64-Square Battlefield

**Viktor:** "Look at the board. 8 ranks — horizontal rows, numbered 1 to 8 from White's side. 8 files — vertical columns, lettered a to h from White's left. Each square has a name. The square in front of your king? **e2**. Remember this — coordinates are the language of chess."

**You:** "Why does White always start at the bottom?"

**Viktor:** *smirks* "Tradition. Also, arrogance. White moves first, you see. Now — the most important rule of board setup: **white on right**. The corner square h1 must be a light square. If you set it up wrong, every game you play is a lie."

blocks.output: Starting position displayed. White pieces on ranks 1-2, Black on ranks 7-8. The board is correctly oriented with 'white on right' — h1 is a light square. Coordinates visible on all sides.

blocks.alt: Standard chessboard with coordinates and starting position
blocks.caption: The battlefield: 64 squares, 32 warriors, infinite possibilities.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 2D chessboard diagram — Standard orientation with White at bottom. Coordinates (a1-h8) clearly labeled on all four sides. Pieces in starting position using Merida-style icons. Light squares in warm cream (#F0D9B5), dark squares in wood brown (#B58863). Subtle drop shadows on pieces. Clean, professional instructional style. A small arrow pointing to h1 with label 'Light square — White on right!'
The Royal Family: King and Queen

**Viktor:** "The king is the soul of your army. He moves one square — any direction. Pathetic, yes? But lose him, and you lose everything. He is the **only piece you cannot sacrifice**.

The queen? She is your nuclear weapon. Any distance, any straight line — horizontal, vertical, diagonal. She is worth **nine pawns**. But remember: **power creates blindness**. Beginners fall in love with their queen and lose her to a knight. I have seen grown men cry."

**You:** "Where do they start?"

**Viktor:** "Queen on her own color. White queen on **d1** — a light square. Black queen on **d8** — dark square. The kings stand beside them: **e1** and **e8**. A king and queen, side by side. Romantic, no? Until the pawns advance and the bloodshed begins."

blocks.output: Board showing only kings and queens in starting positions. Demonstrates 'queen on her own color' rule. White queen on light d1, Black queen on dark d8. Kings adjacent on e-files.

blocks.value: The Heavy Artillery: Rooks and Bishops

**Viktor:** "Rooks are your tanks. They roll forward any distance — horizontal or vertical. Five pawns each. They hate the beginning of the game, blocked by pawns like traffic in Moscow. But in the endgame? When files open? **Two rooks on the 7th rank can make a grandmaster weep.**

Bishops are snipers. Diagonal only, any distance. Also three pawns. But here is their tragedy: **each bishop is colorblind**. The light-squared bishop never touches a dark square. Ever. This is why the **bishop pair** — having both — is precious. Together, they see everything. Alone, each is half-blind."

**You:** "So bishops are weaker than rooks?"

**Viktor:** "In the open game? Sometimes a bishop is worth more. In a closed position, where pawns block diagonals? The rook dominates. Chess is not mathematics. It is **context**."

blocks.output: Board showing White rooks on a1, h1 and bishops on c1, f1. Demonstrates starting positions and movement patterns. Light/dark square bishop limitation concept introduced.

blocks.value: The Knight: The Jumper

**Viktor:** *picks up a knight, spins it* "This is my favorite piece. The knight moves in an **L-shape**: two squares in one direction, then one square sideways. Or one, then two. It is the **only piece that jumps over others**. Pawns, kings, queens — the knight leaps over them all like a Cossack over a fence.

Three pawns in value. But its power is **geometry**, not speed. In the center, a knight commands **eight squares**. In the corner? **Two squares**. This is the first strategic lesson: **pieces are stronger in the center**."

*He places a knight on d5.*

blocks.output: Board showing knight on d5 with all 8 possible destination squares marked with asterisks. Demonstrates L-shaped movement pattern and center vs. corner power difference.

blocks.alt: Knight on d5 showing all 8 possible moves
blocks.caption: A knight in the center is a spider — it touches every part of the web.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 2D chessboard diagram — Knight on d5 with all 8 destination squares highlighted in green circles. L-shaped movement arrows from d5 to each destination. A small comparison inset showing a knight on h1 with only 2 moves (green circles on f2, g3). Label: 'Center = 8 squares' vs 'Corner = 2 squares'. Clean instructional style with subtle knight piece glow effect.
The Pawn: The Soul of Chess

**Viktor:** *leans forward, voice dropping* "Philidor called the pawn **the soul of chess**. One point in value. Moves forward one square. Captures diagonally. On its first move, it may advance **one OR two squares**. It never retreats. **A pawn's decision is forever.**

But here is its secret power: reach the 8th rank, and it **promotes** — becomes a queen, rook, bishop, or knight. Usually a queen. A humble pawn can become royalty. This is why pawn structure — how your pawns stand together — determines the character of the entire game.

And one more thing: because it captures diagonally, a pawn **guards squares it cannot move to**. The e-pawn on e2 guards d3 and f3. It is a soldier and a sentinel."

*He sets up pawns on the second rank.*

blocks.output: Board showing White pawns on rank 2. Demonstrates forward movement, diagonal capture capability, and guard squares. Shows that pawns capture differently than they move — a fundamental chess concept.

blocks.value: Your First Lesson: The Center

**Viktor:** "Before you leave today, one golden rule: **control the center**. The squares d4, d5, e4, e5 — these are the heart of the board. A piece in the center attacks more squares. A pawn in the center controls more territory. Every opening in history fights for these four squares.

Your first move? **1.e4** or **1.d4**. Move the king's pawn or queen's pawn two squares. Claim the center. Announce your presence."

*He resets the board and plays 1.e4.*

blocks.output: Position after 1.e4. White pawn on e4 controls d5 and f5. The board comes alive — pieces now have paths to develop. This single move has started more world championship games than any other.

blocks.caption: 1.e4 — The move that has launched a million battles. The center belongs to White.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 2D chessboard diagram — Standard starting position with White pawn advanced from e2 to e4. Green highlighted squares on d5 and f5 showing controlled center squares. Red arrows from e4 pointing to d5 and f5. Blue arrows showing future development paths for knight (g1-f3) and bishop (f1-c4 or b5). Clean instructional style with '1.e4' notation prominently displayed. Small annotation: 'The most played move in chess history.'

**Viktor:** "Good. You have learned the alphabet. Now go home. Practice setting up the board blindfolded. When you can place every piece in the dark, return. Next time, we discuss the special moves — castling, en passant, promotion. And I will tell you the story of how I lost a world championship because I forgot about en passant."

*He turns back to his board, already lost in a position.*

**Viktor:** *without looking up* "Oh, and one more thing: **never touch a piece unless you intend to move it**. The touch-move rule is not a suggestion. It is law."

blocks.question: Viktor says: 'A knight in the center commands how many squares?'
blocks.explanation: A knight in the center of the board (like d5) can reach 8 squares. From the edge it reaches 4-6, and from the corner only 2. This is why central control is so powerful — pieces gain maximum activity.

blocks.question: Which piece can jump over other pieces, according to Viktor?
blocks.explanation: The knight is the only piece that can jump over other pieces — friend or foe. Viktor calls it 'the only piece that jumps over others like a Cossack over a fence.' This makes it uniquely powerful in blocked positions.

blocks.question: Viktor explains that the pawn is 'the soul of chess.' Select all true statements about pawns:
options: A pawn moves forward one square (or two on its first move)
A pawn can move backward in emergencies
A pawn promotes when it reaches the opposite end
blocks.explanation: Pawns move forward 1 square (or 2 on first move), capture diagonally, never move backward, and promote on the 8th rank. They are worth 1 point, not 5. Viktor emphasizes that 'a pawn's decision is forever' because it never retreats.

blocks.question: Viktor's golden rule: Which four squares form 'the heart of the board' that every opening fights for? (Answer in coordinate notation, separated by commas)
blocks.explanation: The central squares d4, d5, e4, and e5 are the most important squares on the board. A piece in the center controls more territory, which is why 1.e4 and 1.d4 are the most popular opening moves — they fight for central control immediately.
